title: Software & Operating Systems
summary: System vs application vs utility software, what an OS does, Windows features, and file systems. Classification (odd-one-out) questions are the most frequent pattern here.

subtopics.title: Types of software: system, application, utility
subtopics.concept: Every program is one of three kinds. **System software** runs the machine. **Utility software** keeps the machine clean and safe. **Application software** does the user's own work. Software is also grouped by licence: freeware, shareware, open source and proprietary.

tricks.title: SUApp test
tricks.body: Ask who the program serves. The machine means system. Cleaning or protecting the machine means utility. The user's own job means application. Windows is system, antivirus is a utility, Excel is an application.

example.q: Disk Defragmenter is which type of software?
steps: It does not run the machine.
It does not make user documents.

tricks.title: Licence four-word key
tricks.body: Freeware is free forever but closed. Shareware is a sample first. Open source has open code. Proprietary means pay.

example.q: Linux is which kind of software by licence?
steps: That is the mark of open source.

mistakes.wrong: Counting device drivers as application software.
mistakes.right: Drivers serve the hardware, so they are system software.

mistakes.wrong: Calling an antivirus an operating system.
mistakes.right: An antivirus maintains and protects the machine. It is a utility.
Freeware costs nothing, but its source code stays closed.
Shareware is a free trial. You pay to keep using it.

subtopics.notes:
### The three classes of software
Ask one question about any program: **who does it serve?**

| Class | Serves | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **System software** | The machine itself | Operating systems (Windows, Linux, macOS, Android), **device drivers**, **firmware/BIOS**, language translators (compiler, interpreter, assembler) |
| **Utility software** | Maintenance of the machine | Antivirus, disk defragmenter, disk cleanup, backup tools, file compressors, file manager, screen saver |
| **Application software** | The user's task | MS Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Chrome, Photoshop, games, WhatsApp, Tally |

> **Tip:** Use the **SUApp** test. Does it **S**erve the machine (system), **U**nclog it (utility), or do the user's **App** work (application)?

### Two boundary cases
Exams love the programs that sit near the border.

- A **device driver** is system software. You install it like an app. But it only teaches the OS to talk to one piece of hardware, such as a printer.
- A **utility** keeps the machine healthy. It does not make user documents. An **application** makes the user's output.

> **Watch:** Firmware is software burned into a hardware chip, such as the BIOS chip. It is system software too.

### Utility software
A utility is a small maintenance tool. Learn each job.

| Utility | Job |
|---|---|
| Antivirus | Finds and removes malware |
| Disk Defragmenter | Joins scattered pieces of files on a hard disk so reading is faster |
| Disk Cleanup | Deletes temporary and junk files to free space |
| Backup utility | Keeps a second copy of important data |
| Compression tool (WinZip, 7-Zip, WinRAR) | Shrinks files into smaller archives and opens them |
| File manager | Copies, moves, renames and organises files |

### Two kinds of application software
- **General purpose:** made for many users and many jobs. Examples: MS Office, browsers, media players.
- **Application-specific (custom):** made for one job. Examples: a payroll system, a railway reservation system.

### Licence types
A licence says how you may use a program. These four are one-mark favourites.

| Type | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Freeware** | Free of cost, but the **source code stays closed** | Adobe Reader |
| **Shareware** | Free trial first, then you pay | WinZip |
| **Open source** | Source code is available | Linux, LibreOffice, Firefox |
| **Proprietary** | Paid licence, closed source | MS Office |

> **Rule:** Free of **cost** is not the same as open **source**. Freeware is free, but nobody can see its code.

> **Tip:** **F**reeware = **F**ree forever. **S**hareware = **S**ample first. **O**pen source = **O**pen code. **P**roprietary = **P**ay.

revision: System = the machine: OS, drivers, BIOS/firmware, translators.
Utility = maintenance: antivirus, defragmenter, cleanup, backup, compression.
Application = the user's task: Word, Chrome, games, payroll.
Drivers and firmware are system software, not applications.
Freeware = free but closed source. Open source = code available (Linux, Firefox).
Shareware = try first, pay later. Proprietary = paid and closed (MS Office).

subtopics.title: Operating system functions, types and booting
subtopics.concept: The **operating system (OS)** is system software. It manages the hardware and gives programs a place to run. It handles processes, memory, files, devices, security and the user screen. The **kernel** is its core. **Booting** is the start-up of the OS.

tricks.title: PMF-SUIE services
tricks.body: The OS gives Process, Memory, File, Security, User interface and Error handling. A 'manage the machine' answer is OS work. Computing payroll is application work.

example.q: Which OS service gives RAM to programs?
steps: RAM work belongs to memory management.

tricks.title: Boot words
tricks.body: Cold boot starts from a cold, switched-off machine. Warm boot restarts without a power cut. POST always comes first.

example.q: Restarting a running computer is called

mistakes.right: Multiprogramming keeps many programs in RAM. Time-sharing gives each user a slice of CPU time.

mistakes.wrong: Saying the shell stays in memory as the OS core.
mistakes.right: The kernel is the core that stays in memory. The shell is the interface.

mistakes.wrong: Putting the boot loader before POST.
mistakes.right: The order is POST, boot loader, kernel, login.

mistakes.wrong: Calling a restart a cold boot.
mistakes.right: A cold boot starts from power off. A restart is a warm boot.

mistakes.wrong: Thinking iOS runs on many brands of phone.
mistakes.right: iOS is Apple's mobile OS. Android runs on the Linux kernel.

subtopics.notes:
### What an operating system is
The **operating system (OS)** manages all hardware and software. It gives applications a platform to run on. It is the first big program loaded, and it stays in memory until shutdown. Without an OS, the machine is only electronics.

### The services an OS provides
| Service | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Process management** | Decides which waiting program gets the CPU next (scheduling) |
| **Memory management** | Gives RAM to programs and takes it back. **Virtual memory** uses the disk as extra RAM |
| **File management** | Folders, names, saving and finding files through the file system |
| **Device management** | Talks to hardware through **drivers** |
| **Security** | Usernames, passwords and permissions |
| **User interface** | The screen you work on: GUI (Windows) or command line (DOS) |

The OS also handles errors, networking and resource allocation.

> **Tip:** The six main services spell PMF-SUIE: **P**rocess, **M**emory, **F**ile, **S**ecurity, **U**ser interface, **E**rror handling.

### Types of operating systems
| Type | Idea | Where you meet it |
|---|---|---|
| Single-user, single-task | One user, one program at a time | Old MS-DOS |
| Single-user, multitasking | One user, many programs at once | Windows on a PC |
| **Multi-user** | Many users share one machine | UNIX/Linux servers |
| **Multiprogramming** | Several programs sit in RAM. The CPU switches when one waits for input or output | Server systems |
| **Time-sharing** | CPU time is cut into small slices shared among users | Mainframes |
| **Real-time (RTOS)** | Must answer within a fixed deadline | Missiles, robots, medical devices |
| **Distributed** | Many networked machines act as one | Data centres |
| **Embedded** | A small OS built into a device | Washing machine, router |
| **Mobile** | Made for smartphones | Android, iOS |

> **Rule:** In a real-time system, a late answer counts as a failure.

### Kernel and shell
- **Kernel:** the core of the OS. It always stays in memory. It does scheduling, memory work and device work.
- **Shell:** the outer layer. It takes your commands and passes them to the kernel. It can be a **CLI** (typed commands) or a **GUI** (desktop).

Picture the kernel as the engine and the shell as the steering wheel.

### Booting
Booting means starting the OS.

- **Cold boot:** power on from the off state.
- **Warm boot:** restart without cutting power.

The steps run in a fixed order.

1. Power on. The CPU jumps to the **BIOS/UEFI** firmware.
2. **POST** (Power-On Self-Test) checks the hardware.
3. BIOS/UEFI finds the boot device.
4. The **boot loader** loads the **kernel** into RAM.
5. The OS takes charge and the login screen appears.

> **Watch:** POST always comes first. The order is POST, boot loader, kernel, login.

subtopics.title: Windows OS features
subtopics.concept: **Microsoft Windows** is a single-user, multitasking OS with a graphical screen (GUI). Windows 10 came in 2015 and Windows 11 in 2021. Learn the main features, the built-in tools and the small accessory programs.

tricks.title: Plug and Play
tricks.body: Plug and Play means the OS detects and sets up new hardware by itself. The phrase 'automatically detected' in a question points to PnP.

example.q: Which Windows feature sets up a newly attached printer automatically?
steps: Automatic hardware setup is Plug and Play.

tricks.title: Task Manager shortcut
tricks.body: The direct route to Task Manager is Ctrl+Shift+Esc. Ctrl+Alt+Del opens a security menu first. Exams ask for the direct one.

example.q: Which shortcut opens Task Manager directly?
steps: The direct key set is the other one.

mistakes.wrong: Choosing Ctrl+Alt+Del as the direct Task Manager shortcut.
Thinking Shift+Delete moves a file to the Recycle Bin.
mistakes.right: Shift+Delete skips the Recycle Bin. The file is deleted permanently.

mistakes.wrong: Saying Notepad can bold text or insert pictures.
mistakes.right: Notepad is plain text only. WordPad gives simple formatting.

mistakes.wrong: Using Device Manager to end a stuck program.
mistakes.right: Task Manager ends stuck programs. Device Manager lists hardware and drivers.

mistakes.wrong: Saying iOS runs on any phone.
mistakes.right: iOS runs only on Apple devices.

subtopics.notes:
### What Windows is
**Microsoft Windows** is a **single-user, multitasking, GUI-based** OS. Windows 10 came in **2015**. Windows 11 came in **2021**. The desktop you see is the graphical shell. The kernel behind it does the real work.

### Main features
Each row is a one-mark question.

| Feature | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **GUI** | You work with **W**indows, **I**cons, **M**enus and a **P**ointer (WIMP), not typed commands |
| **Multitasking** | Many programs run at the same time |
| **Plug and Play (PnP)** | New hardware is found and set up automatically |
| **File management** | Files and folders are browsed in **File Explorer** |
| **Recycle Bin** | Deleted files land here first. **Shift+Delete** skips it |
| **User accounts** | Administrator or Standard, with a password or PIN |

> **Tip:** The words "detected automatically" in a question mean Plug and Play.

### Built-in tools
| Tool | Job | Shortcut |
|---|---|---|
| **Task Manager** | Shows processes, performance and start-up. Ends stuck programs | **Ctrl+Shift+Esc** |
| **Control Panel / Settings** | System settings. Windows 10 and 11 use the Settings app | |
| **Device Manager** | Lists hardware and drivers | |
| **File Explorer** | Browse, copy, move and rename files | **Win+E** |
| **Disk Management** | Partition and format drives | |
| **Windows Defender** | Built-in antivirus and firewall | |
| **Windows Update** | Keeps patches current | |
| **Command Prompt / PowerShell** | Typed commands (CLI) | |

> **Watch:** Ctrl+Shift+Esc opens Task Manager directly. Ctrl+Alt+Del opens a security menu first.

### More Windows features
- **Virtual desktops:** several desktops on one PC (Win+Ctrl+D).
- **Snap:** places a window at a screen edge (Win+arrow key).
- **OneDrive:** cloud sync.
- **BitLocker:** disk encryption, in Pro editions.

### Picking the right tool
Match the problem to the tool. Take three cases.

1. A program has frozen. Open **Task Manager** and end it.
2. A new printer is not working. Open **Device Manager** and check its driver.
3. You want to change the display or sound. Open **Settings** (Control Panel in older versions).

> **Example:** Files are deleted by mistake with a normal Delete. Open the **Recycle Bin** and restore them. With Shift+Delete, this is not possible.

### Accessories
- **Notepad:** plain text only. No bold, no pictures. It saves .txt files.
- **WordPad:** rich text with simple formatting. It was removed in Windows 11.
- **Paint:** simple drawing and picture editing.
- **Calculator** and **Snipping Tool:** small single-purpose apps.

### Desktop and mobile systems
- **Android:** made by **Google**. Built on the **Linux kernel**. Open source at its core.
- **iOS:** **Apple's** mobile OS. Closed source. Runs only on Apple devices.
- **Desktop trio:** Windows, macOS, Linux.

> **Note:** Android and iOS are the two mobile names exams ask most.

subtopics.title: File systems and file management
subtopics.concept: A **file system** is the set of rules an OS uses to name, store and find files on a disk. FAT32, exFAT and NTFS are the three most asked. FAT32 cannot hold a single file larger than 4 GB.

tricks.title: FAT32 four-GB wall
tricks.body: FAT32 cannot hold a single file bigger than 4 GB. This is the classic exam line. NTFS and exFAT do not have this limit.

example.q: A 5 GB video will not copy to a FAT32 pen drive. Why?
steps: FAT32 has a 4 GB single-file limit.
example.answer: FAT32 limits a file to 4 GB. Use NTFS or exFAT.

tricks.title: Wildcards
tricks.body: The question mark masks exactly one character. The asterisk masks any number. So *.docx finds all Word files.

example.q: Which wildcard stands for any number of characters?
steps: The other symbol is the asterisk.

mistakes.wrong: Thinking FAT32 can store a 6 GB movie.
mistakes.right: FAT32 stops at 4 GB per file. Use exFAT or NTFS.
? matches exactly one character. Use * for any number.

mistakes.wrong: Thinking a format makes the disk bigger or repairs files.
mistakes.right: Formatting lays down a file system. It does not add space.

mistakes.wrong: Using \ or : in a file name.
Thinking move leaves a copy behind.
mistakes.right: Copy leaves the original. Move removes it from the old place.

subtopics.notes:
### What a file system does
A **file system** is the OS's rulebook for a disk. It says how files are named, stored in folders, found again and protected. **Formatting** a drive writes this rulebook onto it.

### File systems compared
| File system | Used by | Key facts |
|---|---|---|
| **FAT32** | Windows 9x, pen drives | Single file up to **4 GB** (minus 1 byte). No permissions, no journaling |
| **exFAT** | Flash drives, cameras | Removes the 4 GB file limit. Light and simple |
| **NTFS** | Modern Windows | Journaling, permissions, encryption, compression, huge files. Default for Windows |
| **ext4** | Linux | Journaling. Default on many distros |
| **APFS** | macOS and iOS | Snapshots and encryption |

Full forms: FAT is File Allocation Table. NTFS is New Technology File System.

> **Rule:** A file larger than 4 GB will not copy into a FAT32 drive. Use exFAT or NTFS.

Windows formats FAT32 volumes only up to about 32 GB. **Journaling** means the system keeps a log, so it can recover after a crash.

### File names and extensions
A file name has two parts: **name.extension**, such as *report.docx*. The extension tells the OS which program opens the file.

| Extension | File type | Extension | File type |
|---|---|---|---|
| .txt | Plain text | .docx | Word document |
| .xlsx | Excel workbook | .pptx | PowerPoint show |
| .pdf | Portable Document | .jpg / .png | Images |
| .mp3 / .wav | Audio | .mp4 | Video |
| .zip | Compressed archive | .html | Web page |
| .exe | Executable program | .bat | Batch (command) file |

> **Watch:** A Windows file name cannot contain any of these: \ / : * ? " < > |

### Wildcards in search
- **?** stands for exactly **one** character. *file?.txt* finds file1.txt and fileA.txt.
- **\*** stands for **any number** of characters. **\*.pdf** finds every PDF.

> **Tip:** `s?t` finds sat, set and sit. `*.docx` finds all Word files.

### Paths and file terms
- **File:** a named collection of related data.
- **Folder (directory):** a container for files.
- **Path:** the address of a file, written drive:\folders\file.ext.
- **Attributes:** read-only, hidden, archive and system.

### Copy, move and delete
- **Copy** (Ctrl+C, Ctrl+V) keeps the original and makes a duplicate.
- **Move** (Ctrl+X, Ctrl+V) shifts the file. The original disappears.
- **Delete** sends the file to the **Recycle Bin**. **Shift+Delete** skips the bin.
- **Properties** (Alt+Enter) shows size, dates and the read-only switch.

Formatting prepares a disk with a file system. It erases the directory, but it does not physically shred the data.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A list mixes an operating system, utilities and applications and asks which is not like the others, or names one program (antivirus, driver, Word) and asks its class.
pyqPatterns.approach: Apply the SUApp test to each option: serves the machine = system (OS, driver, BIOS, compiler), maintains it = utility (antivirus, defragmenter, zip), does the user's work = application (Word, Chrome, games). The odd option is always the one serving a different master.

example.q: Disk Defragmenter, Antivirus, MS Excel, Disk Cleanup — which one is different?
example.solution: MS Excel — the other three are utilities that maintain the machine; Excel is an application that does the user's work.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Which service allots RAM / chooses the next CPU task / manages folders?', 'multiprogramming vs time-sharing vs real-time', 'kernel vs shell'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Match the job to the service: CPU turn = process scheduling, RAM = memory management, folders = file management, passwords = security. For OS types, use the keywords: deadline = real-time, time slices = time-sharing, many programs resident = multiprogramming. Kernel stays in memory; the shell is only the interface.

example.q: Which OS type guarantees a response within a fixed deadline?
example.solution: Real-time operating system (RTOS) — used in missile control, pacemakers and industrial robots where a late answer is a failure.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'What happens first when the computer starts?', 'restarting without power off is called', 'arrange POST, boot loader, kernel, login'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Fix the order: POST (Power-On Self-Test from the BIOS) → boot loader → kernel loads into RAM → login screen. Cold boot = from powered-off; warm boot = restart without cutting power. Any option placing the boot loader before POST is wrong.

example.q: Restarting a running computer through the Restart option is:
example.solution: Warm booting — the power stays on; a cold boot starts from a powered-off state.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Maximum single-file size on FAT32', 'why won't this movie copy to my pen drive', 'which file system has permissions/journaling', 'default file system of Windows'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Three-column memory: FAT32 = 4 GB per file, pendrives; exFAT = FAT32 without the 4-GB wall, big flash media; NTFS = Windows default with permissions and journaling. Scenario stems about a big movie hiding the 4-GB FAT32 ceiling are the most common form.

example.q: The default file system for the C: drive of a modern Windows PC is:
example.solution: NTFS — New Technology File System, with permissions, journaling and huge file support.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Which tool shows CPU usage / stuck programs?', 'which feature auto-detects new hardware?', 'where do you change settings?', 'Notepad vs WordPad'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Tool map: stuck program or CPU/RAM figures → Task Manager (Ctrl+Shift+Esc); hardware and drivers → Device Manager; settings → Control Panel/Settings; junk files → Disk Cleanup. Feature map: auto-detect hardware → Plug and Play; WIMP → GUI. Notepad = plain text, WordPad = formatted text.

example.q: Which Windows tool lists installed hardware with its driver status?
example.solution: Device Manager — every component appears with its driver; problem devices carry a warning mark.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Android is developed by / based on which kernel?', 'iOS runs on which devices?', 'which OS is open source?', 'match OS to maker'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Pin the pairs: Android = Google, Linux kernel, open-source core, many brands; iOS = Apple only, closed source; Windows = Microsoft; macOS = Apple; Linux = open source (Linus Torvalds). Statement versions usually swap the kernel or the owner.

example.q: The Android operating system is built on which kernel?
example.solution: The Linux kernel — Google's Android layers its own system and apps over Linux.

solvedExamples.q: Which of the following is NOT an operating system?
solvedExamples.solution: Oracle is a database management system (application software). Windows 11, Linux and Android are operating systems (Android is built on the Linux kernel).
solvedExamples.shortcut: Scan for a DBMS/browser/office-suite name hiding among OS names - DBMS, Photoshop, Chrome are never operating systems.

solvedExamples.q:
Arrange the booting steps in order:
A. POST  B. Kernel loads  C. Boot loader runs  D. Power switched on
solvedExamples.solution: Power on (D) triggers the POST self-test (A), then the firmware hands control to the boot loader (C), which loads the OS kernel (B).
solvedExamples.shortcut: POST always precedes the loader; the kernel always comes last. Only D-A-C-B satisfies both.

solvedExamples.q: Disk Defragmenter, Disk Cleanup and WinZip are examples of:
solvedExamples.solution: All three maintain or organise the system - defragmenting files, clearing junk, compressing archives - which is the definition of utility software.
solvedExamples.shortcut: If the tool's job is 'clean, compress, protect, back up', it is a utility, not an application.

solvedExamples.q:
Statement 1: NTFS supports file-level security permissions.
Statement 2: A FAT32 volume can store a single file larger than 4 GB.
solvedExamples.solution: NTFS provides per-file/folder permissions, encryption and journaling, so Statement 1 is correct. FAT32 caps any single file at 4 GB (minus 1 byte), so Statement 2 is wrong - large files need NTFS or exFAT.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Remember the 'four-wall' of FAT32; any statement letting FAT32 hold >4-GB files is false.

practice.q: Which of the following is system software?
practice.solution: Windows 11 is an operating system - system software that manages the machine. PowerPoint, Photoshop and Tally are application programs that run on top of an OS.
practice.shortcut: The OS is the platform everything else installs on; look for Windows/Linux/macOS/Android among the options.

practice.q: An antivirus program is best classified as:
practice.solution: Antivirus maintains and protects the system, which places it in utility software (along with defragmenters, backup tools, compressors).
practice.shortcut: 'Protect/maintain/clean' verbs -> utility. Antivirus is the most-asked utility example.

practice.q: The core part of an operating system that remains permanently in main memory is the:
practice.solution: The kernel is the OS core - it manages CPU, memory and devices and always stays resident in RAM. The shell is the user interface layer; BIOS is motherboard firmware; the boot sector merely starts the loading process.
practice.shortcut: Kernel = king in the castle (always resident); shell = gate you talk to.

practice.q: Restarting a computer without switching off the power is called:
practice.solution: Warm booting (restart) reloads the OS without removing power. Cold booting means starting from a fully powered-off state.
practice.shortcut: Warm = restart (machine stays 'warm'); cold = switch on from off.

practice.q: Which OS service decides which waiting program gets the CPU next?
practice.solution: Process management (scheduling) shares CPU time among ready processes. Memory management allocates RAM, file management handles storage, device management drives peripherals.
practice.shortcut: Verb match: 'gets the CPU' -> process scheduling; 'gets RAM' -> memory management.

practice.q: A real-time operating system (RTOS) is most appropriate for:
practice.solution: An RTOS guarantees a response within a strict deadline - essential in missiles, robotics, medical devices and plant control. Payroll, browsing and design have no hard deadlines.
practice.shortcut: Life-or-deadline control jobs -> RTOS; office jobs -> general-purpose OS.

practice.q: Multiprogramming means:
options: Several programs kept in memory with the CPU switching among them
practice.solution: In multiprogramming, multiple programs reside in main memory and the single CPU switches to another whenever the current one waits (e.g. for I/O), raising CPU utilisation. It does not require multiple CPUs or users.
practice.shortcut: One CPU, many resident programs = multiprogramming; time-sliced fairness = time-sharing.

practice.q: The Windows feature that automatically detects and configures a newly connected USB printer is:
practice.solution: Plug and Play lets the OS identify new hardware, install its driver and configure it without manual setup. Hot swapping is only the connect/disconnect-while-running part; overclocking raises clock speed; mirroring is disk redundancy.
practice.shortcut: 'Automatically detects AND configures' = Plug and Play.

practice.q: Deleting a file with Shift+Delete in Windows Explorer:
options: Deletes it permanently without moving it to Recycle Bin
practice.solution: Shift+Delete bypasses the Recycle Bin and permanently deletes the file (after confirmation). Plain Delete sends it to the Recycle Bin.
practice.shortcut: Add Shift = skip the bin. That single fact answers most Recycle-Bin questions.

practice.q: Which utility shows running processes, CPU/RAM usage and startup programs in Windows?
practice.solution: Task Manager (Ctrl+Shift+Esc) displays processes, performance graphs, startup impact and lets you end tasks. Device Manager lists hardware/drivers; Disk Management handles partitions; Event Viewer logs system events.
practice.shortcut: Running apps + performance = Task Manager; hardware + drivers = Device Manager.

practice.q: Notepad, the basic Windows text editor, saves files as:
practice.solution: Notepad writes plain text with no bold/italic formatting - its default extension is .txt. Formatted text needs WordPad or a word processor.
practice.shortcut: No formatting = Notepad; any option promising fonts/bold is WordPad/Word territory.

practice.q: The maximum size of a single file on a FAT32 volume is:
practice.solution: FAT32 cannot store any single file larger than 4 GB (minus 1 byte); NTFS and exFAT lift this limit. This is why pendrives formatted as FAT32 reject large videos.
practice.shortcut: The 'four-wall' of FAT32: 4 GB per file, straight recall.

practice.q: In a Windows file search, the pattern *report*.xlsx will find:
options: All .xlsx files whose names contain the word report
All files of any type containing report
practice.solution: The asterisk matches any number of characters, so *report*.xlsx matches any Excel workbook with 'report' anywhere in its name - e.g. annual-report-2026.xlsx and report-final.xlsx.
practice.shortcut: Prefix * = anything before, suffix * = anything after; .xlsx at the end restricts the type.

practice.q: Android, the mobile operating system, is built on which kernel?
practice.solution: Android uses the Linux kernel at its core with Java/Kotlin application layers on top - a standard exam fact.
practice.shortcut: Android = Linux kernel; iOS/macOS = Darwin (UNIX-based).

practice.q: Which of the following is **application** software?
practice.solution: **MS PowerPoint** produces the user's slides — an application. Windows 11 is an OS, a driver is system software, and the Defragmenter is a utility.
practice.shortcut: Serves the user's task = application.

practice.q: A small program that teaches the operating system how to communicate with a newly attached **printer** is —
practice.solution: A **device driver** is system software — it lets the OS control one specific hardware item. Without the driver, the OS cannot use the printer.
practice.shortcut: Driver = system software, whatever it 'looks like'.

practice.q: Which utility is used to **protect a computer from viruses**?
practice.solution: **Antivirus** software scans, detects and removes malicious programs — the protective member of the utility crew.
practice.shortcut: Virus → antivirus. Cleanup and defrag do other jobs.

practice.q: **WinZip** and **7-Zip** are examples of —
practice.solution: They **compress** one or more files into a smaller archive (.zip) and extract them again — utility software for storage economy and faster transfer.
practice.shortcut: Zip = squeeze.

practice.q: Which utility **automatically deletes temporary files** to free disk space in Windows?
practice.solution: **Disk Cleanup** removes temporary files, cache and Recycle Bin contents to free space. The Defragmenter rearranges files instead; Backup copies data.
practice.shortcut: Space → Cleanup; speed → Defragmenter.

practice.q: Software offered **free for a trial period**, after which payment is required, is called —
practice.solution: **Shareware** = 'sample first': free to try for a limited period or feature set, then you must pay to continue. Freeware is free forever.
practice.shortcut: Share = try, then share the cost.

practice.q: Which statement is **correct**?
options: Open-source software makes its source code available for use and modification
Shareware can never be paid for
practice.solution: **Open source** means the source code is public (Linux, LibreOffice, VLC). Freeware is free of cost but closed source; Windows is proprietary; shareware asks for payment after the trial.
practice.shortcut: Cost-free ≠ source-free — two different freedoms.

practice.q: Which of the following is **NOT** an operating system?
practice.solution: **Photoshop** is an image-editing **application**. Linux, macOS and Android are operating systems.
practice.shortcut: Famous app names are the planted odd ones.

practice.q: Which of the following is an operating system rather than an application?
practice.solution: **Ubuntu** is one of the most widely used **Linux** distributions — an operating system. Chrome, Excel and Adobe Reader are applications.
practice.shortcut: Ubuntu/Fedora/Debian = Linux family = OS.

practice.q:
Consider the statements:
1. The operating system is system software.
2. Firmware is typically stored in a ROM chip.
3. A compiler is application software.
Which are correct?
practice.solution: Statements 1 and 2 are standard. Statement 3 is wrong: a compiler is a **language translator, which is system software** — it serves the machine, not the user's document work.
practice.shortcut: Translators sit on the system-software side of the line.

practice.q:
Consider the statements:
1. Defragmentation speeds up access on traditional hard disks.
2. Disk Cleanup rearranges file fragments.
3. A backup utility protects data against loss.
Which are correct?
practice.solution: Statement 2 swaps the jobs: **Disk Cleanup deletes** junk files; the **Defragmenter** does the rearranging. Statements 1 and 3 are correct.
practice.shortcut: Cleanup deletes, defrag rearranges — never the reverse.

practice.q: Which OS service decides **which waiting program gets the CPU next**?
practice.solution: **Process management** schedules the CPU among all ready programs — choosing who runs next is its daily job.
practice.shortcut: CPU turn-taking = process scheduling.

practice.q: Checking **usernames and passwords** before allowing access is part of which OS service?
practice.solution: **Security** covers user accounts, passwords and permissions — deciding who may enter and what they may touch.
practice.shortcut: Passwords → security.

practice.q: When RAM is full, Windows uses **disk space as extra working memory**. This is called —
practice.solution: **Virtual memory** is disk space acting as an overflow for RAM (page file). It saves the day when RAM runs out but is far slower than real RAM. Cache is a different, much faster thing near the CPU.
practice.shortcut: Disk-as-RAM = virtual memory.

practice.q: A **washing machine** or router contains a small special-purpose OS inside the appliance. This is a(n) —
practice.solution: **Embedded OS** = a compact OS fixed inside an appliance, running one dedicated job for its whole life.
practice.shortcut: Inside the machine = embedded.

practice.q: In a **time-sharing** operating system, the CPU —
options: Runs only one program per day
Is shared among many users/tasks in small time slices
practice.solution: **Time-sharing** cuts CPU time into tiny slices and gives each user or task a slice in rotation — so fast that everyone feels the machine is theirs alone.
practice.shortcut: Slices round the table = time-sharing.

practice.q: **Unix** servers allow **hundreds of users to log in simultaneously** on separate terminals. This capability marks Unix as a —
practice.solution: Many users working at the same instant on one machine defines a **multi-user** operating system (Unix, Linux servers).
practice.shortcut: Many logins at once = multi-user.

practice.q: The **core of the operating system**, which remains permanently in main memory and handles scheduling and devices, is the —
practice.solution: The **kernel** is the OS's in-memory core — it schedules processes, allots memory and drives devices. The shell is only its interface.
practice.shortcut: Kernel = engine, always running.

practice.q: **MS-DOS**, where you typed commands like DIR and COPY on a black screen, used which type of interface?
practice.solution: DOS used a **command-line interface** — you typed commands; no windows, icons or mouse pointer. Windows brought the GUI style.
practice.shortcut: Typed commands = CLI; point-and-click = GUI.

practice.q: The diagnostic routine that checks RAM, keyboard and disks the moment a computer is **switched on** is —
practice.solution: **POST** runs from the BIOS firmware before anything else loads — it beeps if the hardware passes.
practice.shortcut: First check = POST.

practice.q:
Put the booting steps in order:
A. Boot loader runs  B. POST  C. Kernel is loaded into RAM  D. Login screen appears
practice.solution: **POST → boot loader → kernel → login.** The BIOS tests hardware first (POST), then hands over to the boot loader, which loads the OS kernel.
practice.shortcut: Self-test before anything loads.

practice.q: Switching on a computer that was **powered off** is called —
practice.solution: **Cold boot** = the machine starts from a powered-off ('cold') state. **Warm boot** = restarting without cutting the power (the Restart option).
practice.shortcut: Cold = from off; warm = restart.

practice.q:
Consider the statements:
1. Multiprogramming requires multiple CPUs.
2. In multiprogramming, several programs stay in memory while one CPU switches among them.
3. A real-time OS guarantees a response within a deadline.
Which are correct?
practice.solution: Statement 1 is the classic trap — multiprogramming uses **one CPU juggling** resident programs, not many CPUs. Statements 2 and 3 are the correct definitions.
practice.shortcut: One CPU, many programs — multiprogramming in one line.

practice.q:
Consider the statements:
1. POST runs before the boot loader.
2. Warm booting restarts the machine without switching off the power.
3. The BIOS loads the operating system directly into the Recycle Bin.
Which are correct?
practice.solution: Statements 1 and 2 are the standard booting facts. Statement 3 is nonsense — the boot loader loads the **kernel into RAM**; the Recycle Bin is a desktop folder for deleted files.
practice.shortcut: One absurd statement marks the wrong set.

practice.q: Windows is best described as a —
practice.solution: One user at a time, many programs at once (multitasking), and a graphical desktop — the standard three-label description of Windows.
practice.shortcut: One user, many apps, pictures on screen.

practice.q: **Multitasking** means —
options: The OS running several programs at the same time by switching the CPU among them
practice.solution: Multitasking = the OS gives each open program a slice of CPU time so browsing, music and typing all appear simultaneous on one machine.
practice.shortcut: One CPU, many programs, quick switching.

practice.q: The letters of **WIMP**, the classic GUI elements, stand for —
practice.solution: **WIMP** = Windows, Icons, Menus, Pointer — the four visible pieces of every graphical desktop.
practice.shortcut: The desktop shows exactly these four things.

practice.q: Which Windows tool shows **running programs, CPU and memory usage**, and lets you end a stuck application?
practice.solution: **Task Manager** (Ctrl+Shift+Esc) lists processes with their CPU/RAM load and lets you End Task on a 'not responding' app.
practice.shortcut: Stuck app → Task Manager.

practice.q: To **change the desktop background, date-time and user accounts**, you would open —
practice.solution: **Settings (Control Panel)** is where system-wide choices live — display, sound, users, network, date and time.
practice.shortcut: Settings change the machine; tools use it.

practice.q: Which tool **lists all installed hardware along with its drivers** and flags devices that are not working?
practice.solution: **Device Manager** enumerates every hardware component with its driver status — problem devices show a warning mark.
practice.shortcut: Hardware + drivers → Device Manager.

practice.q: How does **WordPad** differ from **Notepad**?
options: WordPad supports basic text formatting; Notepad saves plain text only
Notepad supports formatting; WordPad does not
practice.solution: **Notepad** = pure plain text (.txt). **WordPad** adds bold, fonts and colours (rich text) — a halfway house between Notepad and MS Word.
practice.shortcut: Notepad is a pencil; WordPad is a pen with colours.

practice.q: Which built-in Windows accessory is used for **simple drawing and painting**?
practice.solution: **Paint** — the drawing accessory for sketches and basic image edits. Notepad writes text; Calculator computes; Command Prompt types commands.
practice.shortcut: Paint paints.

practice.q: The **Android** mobile operating system is owned and developed by —
practice.solution: **Google** owns and leads Android (originally built by Android Inc., which Google acquired in 2005); many brands ship it.
practice.shortcut: Android = Google's robot.

practice.q: **iOS**, the mobile operating system, runs only on —
options: Apple devices such as the iPhone and iPad
practice.solution: **iOS/iPadOS** is Apple's closed-source mobile OS, licensed to run **only on Apple hardware**.
practice.shortcut: iOS = 'i' = Apple only.

practice.q:
Consider the statements:
1. Plug and Play needs the user to install drivers manually for every new device.
2. Windows is a single-user multitasking OS.
3. The Recycle Bin catches files deleted from a USB pen drive by ordinary Delete.
Which are correct?
practice.solution: Statement 1 reverses PnP — its whole point is **automatic** detection and configuration. Statement 2 is correct. Statement 3 is wrong: pen-drive deletions usually **bypass the Recycle Bin** (which serves fixed drives).
practice.shortcut: PnP = automatic; Recycle Bin covers fixed drives, not removable ones.

practice.q:
Match the OS to its maker:
A. Android  B. iOS  C. Windows  D. macOS
practice.solution: Android → Google; iOS → Apple; Windows → Microsoft; macOS → Apple. Apple owns two OSes (mobile iOS, desktop macOS).
practice.shortcut: Apple has two; Microsoft has one of each world.

practice.q: Which file system is the **default for the system drive (C:)** of modern Windows installations?
practice.solution: **NTFS** (New Technology File System) has been the Windows default for hard disks and SSDs since Windows XP — it adds permissions and journaling.
practice.shortcut: Windows drives = NTFS; pen drives = FAT32/exFAT.

practice.q: You cannot copy a **5-GB movie** to a pen drive formatted as **FAT32** because —
options: The drive is slower than the disk
FAT32 cannot hold a single file larger than 4 GB
practice.solution: The **4-GB single-file limit** is FAT32's most quoted ceiling. The drive's 16–64 GB total size is irrelevant to this per-file wall.
practice.shortcut: 4 GB — FAT32's four walls.

practice.q: A photographer needs a **64-GB SD card** that stores individual video files larger than 4 GB and still works in cameras. The best format is —
practice.solution: **exFAT** (extended FAT) removes FAT32's 4-GB file limit and stays light enough for cameras and flash media — the standard choice for large SD cards.
practice.shortcut: exFAT = FAT32 grown up.

practice.q: Which feature does **NTFS** support but **FAT32 does not**?
options: File and folder permissions with journaling
practice.solution: NTFS brings **security permissions** and **journaling** (a log that helps recovery after a crash). Folders and long names exist in both systems.
practice.shortcut: NTFS = New Technology = new powers: permissions + journal.

practice.q: In Windows search, the wildcard **?** stands for —
practice.solution: **?** = exactly one character (file?.txt matches file1.txt, fileA.txt). **\*** = any number of characters.
practice.shortcut: One question mark, one letter.

practice.q: The search pattern **\*.pdf** will find —
options: All PDF files in the searched location
practice.solution: The **\*** masks any name, and the extension fixes the type — so every file ending in .pdf is listed.
practice.shortcut: Star = anything, extension decides the type.

practice.q: Which of the following is **NOT a valid** file name in Windows?
practice.solution: The colon (**:**) is one of the forbidden characters (\ / : * ? " < > |) because Windows reserves it for drive letters. The other names are legal.
practice.shortcut: Drive letters use the colon, so file names cannot.

practice.q: To find **all Excel files whose names contain the word 'bank'**, the best search pattern is —
practice.solution: The first * absorbs anything before 'bank', the second anything after it, and .xlsx fixes the type. bank.xlsx matches only that exact name; *bank*.xlsx catches 'bank2026.xlsx' and 'mybank.xlsx' alike.
practice.shortcut: Star on both sides of the word, type at the end.

practice.q: A file named **result.xlsx** was created in —
practice.solution: **.xlsx** is the Excel workbook extension (Word = .docx, PowerPoint = .pptx, plain text = .txt).
practice.shortcut: x is for Excel.

practice.q: **.zip** files are —
options: Compressed archives of one or more files
practice.solution: A **.zip** stores one or more files in compressed form; tools like 7-Zip or Explorer extract the originals.
practice.shortcut: Zip = squeezed bag of files.

practice.q: **PDF** (the extension .pdf) stands for —
practice.solution: **Portable Document Format** — a fixed-layout document that looks identical on every device, opened in readers like Adobe Reader or a browser.
practice.shortcut: P = Portable, always.

practice.q: Which statement about **formatting** a disk is correct?
options: It increases the disk's storage capacity
It prepares the disk by laying down a file system
practice.solution: Formatting writes a fresh **file system** (and erases existing file records) so the OS can store and retrieve files. It does not enlarge capacity, repair files or defragment.
practice.shortcut: Format = new rulebook, not new space.

practice.q:
Consider the statements:
1. NTFS keeps a journal that helps recovery after a sudden power cut.
2. exFAT has the same 4-GB single-file limit as FAT32.
3. A file name in Windows may contain the * character.
Which are correct?
practice.solution: Statement 1 is NTFS's headline safety feature. Statement 2 is wrong — removing the 4-GB wall is exFAT's purpose. Statement 3 is wrong: * is a reserved wildcard character, illegal in names.
practice.shortcut: One right fact, two reversed classics — read slowly.
